articles.title: Manipur boxer Lairenlakpam Ambekar Meetei makes history with India's first Youth Olympics gold
articles.content: News Manipur Manipur boxer Lairenlakpam Ambekar Meetei makes history with India's first Youth Olympics gold Manipur boxer Lairenlakpam Ambekar Meetei makes history with India's first Youth Olympics gold Lairenlakpam Ambekar Meetei defeated Ireland's Jubani Kristian 3-2 in the men's 50kg final. His victory delivered India's first Youth Olympics boxing gold and lifted the medal tally to nine. Advertisement India TodayNE Nov 13, 2026 , Updated Nov 13, 2026, 8:34 AM IST Follow us: Story highlights India's medal tally rose to nine, placing the contingent ninth overall Gunjan reached women's final after beating Lily Bassett 4-1 in semi-finals Shourya Ambure became first Indian woman with Youth Olympics athletics medal Manipur's Lairenlakpam Ambekar Meetei scripted history on November 12 by becoming the first Indian boxer to win a gold medal at the Youth Olympic Games, defeating Ireland's Jubani Kristian 3-2 in the men's 50kg final at Dakar 2026. The victory not only marked a landmark moment for Indian boxing but also secured the country's first gold medal at the ongoing edition of the Games, taking India's overall medal tally to nine, the Boxing Federation of India (BFI) said in a press note. India had never won a boxing gold at the Youth Olympic Games before Ambekar Meetei's triumph. The country now has one gold, three silver and five bronze medals, placing it ninth in the overall standings. India could add another gold to its tally later on Thursday, with Gunjan set to compete in the women's boxing final at 10.30 pm IST. She entered the title clash after defeating Great Britain's Lily Bassett 4-1 in the semi-finals. Ambekar Meetei had also delivered a dominant performance in the last-four stage, defeating Colombia's Izzon Jeffrey Galea Arevalo 5-0 to book his place in the final. India's medal haul at Dakar has come across several disciplines, including athletics, wrestling, judo, badminton, swimming and wushu. In athletics, Shourya Ambure won bronze in the women's 100m hurdles with a personal best of 13.59 seconds, becoming the first Indian woman to win an athletics medal at the Youth Olympic Games. Taniya secured silver in the women's 75kg wrestling category, giving India its first-ever youth wrestling medal at the competition. She lost 1-2 to China's Min Zhao, the 2025 U17 World Wrestling Championships gold medallist in the 69kg category, in the final. Khushbu Rajakbhai Darjada in women's 63kg judo and Tanvi Patri in badminton also won silver medals. Swimming added three medals to India's tally. Dhinidhi Desinghu claimed bronze in both the women's 100m and 200m freestyle events, becoming the first Indian athlete to win multiple medals at a single edition of the Youth Olympic Games. Tirthank Pegu also secured bronze in the men's 200m butterfly, becoming the first Indian male swimmer to win a medal at the event. Rajkumari Lanchenbi Chanu completed India's medal tally in wushu with a bronze in the women's changquan combined event. articles.title: India's Journey of Discovery and Innovation in Space - Rising Kashmir
articles.content: Opinion India's Journey of Discovery and Innovation in Space The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has developed rockets and satellites that support communication, navigation, weather forecasting and early warnings of natural disasters ER. SUHAIB BAKSHI 13 Nov 2026 02:18 IST Follow Us BEYOND THE SKY Space has always inspired human curiosity. From observing the stars to developing spacecraft, generations have sought to understand the universe and humanity's place within it. Today, advances in scientific research and technology are making it possible to explore space in ways once considered beyond reach. India is now an active part of this wider journey of discovery, with its space programme entering an important new phase. India's early space research began with modest facilities and ambitious scientific goals. On 21 November 1963, a research rocket carrying instruments to study the upper atmosphere was launched from Thumba in Kerala. India's first indigenous sounding rocket followed in 1967. Such rockets carry scientific instruments into the atmosphere to collect information. These early initiatives helped develop the knowledge and experience needed for a long-term space programme. Vikram Sarabhai, recognised as the father of India's space programme, believed that space technology could help address practical needs on Earth. His vision placed importance on communication, education, weather forecasting and the responsible use of scientific knowledge. That approach continues to influence the development of space technology. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has developed rockets and satellites that support communication, navigation, weather forecasting and early warnings of natural disasters. Its scientific missions have also contributed to the understanding of the Moon, Mars and the Sun. Chandrayaan-3 reached the Moon's southern high-latitude region on 23 August 2023, and its Pragyan rover conducted scientific studies on the lunar surface. Mangalyaan entered Mars orbit in September 2014, while Aditya-L1 reached its observing position in January 2024 to study the Sun. The space sector is also seeing growing participation from private Indian companies, which are contributing to the development of launch vehicles, satellites, engines and space-based services. This wider participation is creating opportunities for engineers, scientists, researchers and young entrepreneurs. Among the companies working in this field is Skyroot Aerospace, founded in Hyderabad in 2018. In November 2022, its Vikram-S rocket completed a suborbital test flight, demonstrating its rocket technology without placing a satellite into orbit. On 18 July 2026, the company's Vikram-1 made its maiden orbital launch, placing two satellites, Skyroot's SCOPE and Grahaa Space's SOLARAS S3, into low Earth orbit. An orbital launch, on the other hand, gives a satellite the speed and direction needed to continue travelling around Earth. These missions marked important stages in the development of Skyroot's launch vehicles. Agnikul Cosmos, based in Chennai, is developing small rockets designed to carry satellites. In May 2024, it tested Agnibaan SOrTeD using a single-piece engine made through 3D printing, a process in which an object is built layer by layer from a digital design.
